objectives.summary: Azure managed disks offer several encryption layers. Server-side encryption (SSE) is always on and can use customer-managed keys through a disk encryption set. Encryption at host extends SSE to temp disks and caches end to end. Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) encrypts inside the guest with BitLocker or DM-Crypt and is scheduled to retire on 15 September 2028. Confidential disk encryption binds keys to a confidential VM's TPM. Know what each layer covers and when to choose it.

keyFacts.fact: SSE always encrypts OS and data disks at rest with 256-bit AES and can use customer-managed keys when configured with a disk encryption set (DES); it doesn't encrypt temp disks or disk caches.
Encryption at host encrypts temp disks and OS/data disk caches at rest and keeps data encrypted as it flows to storage; temp disks use only platform-managed keys, and it doesn't consume VM CPU.

Azure Disk Encryption is scheduled for retirement on 15 September 2028; after that, ADE-encrypted disks fail to unlock on reboot. Use encryption at host for new VMs or confidential VMs with OS disk encryption.

Encryption at host requires registering the EncryptionAtHost feature in the Microsoft.Compute namespace; enable it with az vm create --encryption-at-host or az vm update --set securityProfile.encryptionAtHost=true, and the VM must be deallocated to disable it.

For customer-managed keys, the Key Vault or Managed HSM must be in the same region as the disks and must have purge protection enabled; if the key is disabled, deleted or expired, VMs using it automatically shut down.
Confidential disk encryption binds disk encryption keys to the VM's TPM so protected content is accessible only to that VM; it applies to the OS disk, with temp disk encryption as an opt-in.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Virtual machines > (VM) > Disks > Additional settings > Encryption at host; Azure portal > Disk Encryption Sets

lab.title: Create a VM with encryption at host using platform-managed keys
steps: Open Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) in a trial subscription.
Run: az feature register --namespace Microsoft.Compute --name EncryptionAtHost
Run az feature show --namespace Microsoft.Compute --name EncryptionAtHost until the state is Registered.
Run: az group create -n rg-enc-lab -l eastus
Run: az vm create -g rg-enc-lab -n vmEnc1 --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_D2s_v5 --encryption-at-host --generate-ssh-keys
Run: az vm show -g rg-enc-lab -n vmEnc1 --query securityProfile.encryptionAtHost -o tsv
lab.verify: The final command returns true, and in Defender for Cloud the VM's disk encryption status is reported as healthy.

questions.question: The EncryptionAtHost feature is already registered on your subscription. You need to deploy a Linux VM that uses encryption at host with a customer-managed key in Azure Key Vault. Put the steps in order.
items: Create a Key Vault with purge protection enabled
Create an RSA key in the Key Vault
Create a disk encryption set that references the key URL
Grant the disk encryption set's managed identity get, wrapkey and unwrapkey permissions on the Key Vault
Create the VM with --encryption-at-host and the disk encryption set specified for its disks
questions.explanation: The key can only be created in an existing vault (purge protection is mandatory for disk encryption), and the disk encryption set needs the key URL, so the key must exist first. Creating the disk encryption set creates its system-assigned identity, which must then be granted get, wrapkey and unwrapkey on the vault before disks can use it. Finally, the VM is created with encryption at host and the disk encryption set. Any other sequence fails because a dependency doesn't exist yet.

objectives.summary: Azure Bastion provides RDP and SSH to VMs over TLS on port 443 without public IPs on the VMs. Choosing the SKU is the key planning decision. Developer is free and supports one VM at a time with no peering. Basic gives two fixed instances. Standard adds native client, shareable links, IP-based connect, custom ports, file transfer and host scaling. Premium adds session recording and private-only deployment.

keyFacts.fact: Basic, Standard and Premium require a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet of /26 or larger; Developer uses shared infrastructure and needs neither the subnet nor a public IP.
Developer SKU supports one VM connection at a time and doesn't support virtual network peering; Basic has a fixed two instances (40 RDP / 80 SSH sessions).
Standard adds native client (Azure CLI) connections, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom inbound ports, file upload/download and host scaling from 2 to 50 instances.
Premium adds graphical session recording (stored in a blob container, authenticated with a SAS URL or a managed identity (preview)) and private-only deployment with no public IP.
Session recording isn't available through the native client, and recording storage must not use immutable storage policies or blob versioning.
SKU upgrades take about 10 minutes; downgrading isn't supported, so you must delete and recreate Bastion.

lab.title: Deploy Bastion Standard and connect with the native client
steps: Create a VNet with an AzureBastionSubnet of /26 and a workload subnet containing a Linux VM with no public IP.
Create a Standard SKU public IP, then run: az network bastion create -g rg-bastion-lab -n bas1 --vnet-name vnet1 --public-ip-address bas1-pip --sku Standard --enable-tunneling true
After deployment, run: az network bastion ssh --name bas1 --resource-group rg-bastion-lab --target-resource-id <VM resource ID> --auth-type ssh-key --username azureuser --ssh-key ~/.ssh/id_rsa
In the portal, open the bastion's Sessions page to see the active session.

objectives.summary: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access is a Defender for Servers Plan 2 feature that keeps management ports closed with deny rules and opens them only on approved request, for a limited time and from specific source IPs. It works with NSGs and with Azure Firewall classic rules, and also supports AWS EC2 (preview). Users request access from Defender for Cloud, the VM's Connect page, PowerShell or REST.

keyFacts.fact: JIT requires Defender for Servers Plan 2 and supports Resource Manager VMs and VMs protected by Azure Firewall in the same VNet; classic VMs and firewalls managed by Azure Firewall Manager policies aren't supported.
Defender for Cloud recommends protecting ports 22 (SSH), 3389 (RDP), 5985 and 5986 (WinRM); for each port you set protocol, allowed source IPs and maximum request time.

When a request is approved, Defender for Cloud configures the NSG and Azure Firewall to allow the requested ports from the specified IP for the approved time; when it expires the NSG is restored, new connections are blocked and established connections aren't interrupted.
To request access a user needs Microsoft.Security/locations/jitNetworkAccessPolicies/initiate/action plus read permissions; Set-JitLeastPrivilegedRole script creates a least-privileged role.
PowerShell uses Set-AzJitNetworkAccessPolicy to configure JIT and Start-AzJitNetworkAccessPolicy to request access; a VM shows as Unsupported if it has no NSG or Azure Firewall.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Workload protections > Just-in-time VM access > Not configured / Configured

lab.title: Enable JIT on a VM and request access
steps: Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2 on a trial subscription containing a Windows VM with an NSG.
Open Defender for Cloud > Workload protections > Just-in-time VM access > Not configured, select the VM and choose Enable JIT on VMs.
Keep port 3389, set Allowed source IPs to Per request and Maximum request time to 1 hour, then Save.
Go to the Configured tab, select the VM and choose Request access; select port 3389, My IP, a 1-hour window, then Open ports.
Open the VM's NSG and review the inbound rules.
lab.verify: The NSG shows the JIT deny rule for 3389 plus a temporary allow rule for your IP while the request is active; after the window, the NSG returns to its previous state.

objectives.summary: Azure Arc-enabled servers project on-premises and other-cloud machines into Azure through the Connected Machine agent, so Defender for Cloud, Azure Policy and Machine Configuration can manage them. Arc also gives local security controls that only a local admin can change: extension allowlists and blocklists, monitor mode, and disabling the guest configuration agent or remote connectivity. These are important for Tier 0 servers such as domain controllers.

keyFacts.fact: Microsoft recommends onboarding non-Azure machines as Azure Arc-enabled servers so they get the full set of Defender for Servers features; the Arc Connected Machine agent is installed on them.

Extension allowlists and blocklists are set locally with azcmagent config set extensions.allowlist/blocklist; nobody in Azure, even an Owner or Global Administrator, can override them. Allowlists are preferred because they block new extensions by default.

Monitor mode (azcmagent config set config.mode monitor) applies a Microsoft-managed allowlist of monitoring and security extensions, disables remote connectivity and disables the machine configuration agent.

For Tier 0 assets, consider a dedicated subscription, disabling incoming connections (incomingconnections.enabled false), disabling guest configuration, and allowlisting only needed extensions such as AMA and MDE.Windows.
The Custom Script Extension and Run Command run as Local System or root; block them unless needed because attackers could use them to run malicious code.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Azure Arc > Machines > Add/Create > Add a machine; local agent: azcmagent config

lab.title: Lock down the Arc agent on a test server
steps: Onboard a test Windows or Linux server to Azure Arc using the script generated at Azure Arc > Machines > Add a machine.
On the server run: azcmagent show and confirm the agent is Connected.
Run: azcmagent config set extensions.allowlist "Microsoft.Azure.Monitor/AzureMonitorLinuxAgent,Microsoft.Azure.AzureDefenderForServers/MDE.Linux" (use the Windows equivalents on Windows).
Run: azcmagent config set guestconfiguration.enabled false
Run: azcmagent config list to review the settings.
From the Azure portal, try installing the Custom Script Extension on the machine.
lab.verify: azcmagent config list shows the allowlist and guest configuration disabled, and the Custom Script Extension install is reported as failed.

objectives.summary: Defender for Servers protects Windows and Linux machines in Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises. You enable it on a subscription and choose Plan 1 or Plan 2. AWS and GCP machines are onboarded through Defender for Cloud multicloud connectors, which can auto-provision Azure Arc. On-premises machines should be onboarded as Arc-enabled servers. Plan 1 is focused on Defender for Endpoint EDR, while Plan 2 adds agentless scanning, JIT, FIM, premium vulnerability management and the 500 MB data ingestion benefit.

keyFacts.fact: Plan 1 focuses on EDR via the Defender for Endpoint integration; Plan 2 includes Plan 1 and adds agentless scanning, premium Defender Vulnerability Management, file integrity monitoring, JIT access, OS configuration and update assessment, network map and a free data ingestion benefit.

Connecting AWS accounts and GCP projects onboards their machines as Azure Arc-enabled VMs by default; Arc auto-provisioning for AWS requires the Owner role on the Azure subscription and the AWS SSM Agent on EC2 instances.

If on-premises machines are onboarded by directly installing Defender for Endpoint instead of Arc, Plan 1 functionality is available, and Plan 2 only adds premium Defender Vulnerability Management features.
After you enable a plan, a 30-day trial starts that can't be stopped, paused or extended.
Both plans provide the capabilities of Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, including EDR.

To get 500 MB of free daily ingestion per node, enable Plan 2 on the Log Analytics workspace the machines report to; eligible security data must arrive through AMA, the Defender for Endpoint sensor or agentless FIM.

BYOL vulnerability assessment (Qualys, Rapid7) is being deprecated; migrate to Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management.

File integrity monitoring requires Plan 2, isn't on by default, and collects data with the Defender for Endpoint agent (near real time) and agentless scanning (24-hour cadence), storing change events in a Log Analytics workspace.

objectives.summary: Agentless machine scanning takes snapshots of VM disks and analyzes them out of band, so no agent or network connectivity is needed and VM performance isn't affected. It provides software inventory, vulnerability assessment, secrets scanning, EDR configuration checks and, with Plan 2, malware scanning. It's on by default with Defender for Servers Plan 2 or Defender CSPM, and you can exclude machines using tags.

keyFacts.fact: Agentless scanning is available in Defender CSPM and Defender for Servers Plan 2; malware scanning is only in Defender for Servers Plan 2. It covers Azure VMs, AWS EC2 and GCP compute instances.

Defender for Cloud snapshots the OS and data disks, keeps the copy in the same region, analyzes it in an isolated scanning environment, and deletes the snapshot once metadata is collected (typically minutes).
In Azure, the built-in VM scanner operator role is used; scanning CMK-encrypted disks needs extra Key Vault key read, wrap and unwrap permissions.
Exclude machines by entering tag:value pairs under Environment settings > plan Settings > Agentless scanning for machines > Edit configuration; excluded machines are skipped during discovery.
Only machines that are running during a scheduled scan are scanned; allow up to 24 hours for results after enabling or changing permissions.

objectives.summary: Trusted Launch protects Generation 2 VMs against bootkits, rootkits and kernel malware with Secure Boot, a virtual TPM and boot integrity monitoring. It's selected through the VM's security type (Standard, Trusted launch, or Confidential). Trusted Launch is the default for new Gen2 VMs created in the portal, CLI and PowerShell. Integrity monitoring installs the Guest Attestation extension so Defender for Cloud can attest boot health and alert on failures.

keyFacts.fact: Secure Boot ensures only signed OS boot components (boot loader, kernel, kernel drivers) load; if an image isn't signed by a trusted publisher the VM fails to boot.
The vTPM is TPM 2.0 compliant, runs outside the VM's reach, measures the whole boot chain and enables remote attestation.

Boot integrity monitoring requires Secure Boot and vTPM plus the Guest Attestation extension; enable it in the portal at VM > Configuration > Security type > Integrity monitoring, or with --enable-integrity-monitoring in the CLI.

Defender for Cloud recommends enabling Secure Boot, vTPM and the Guest Attestation extension, and raises a medium-severity alert when VM attestation fails; attestation fails if Secure Boot is disabled.
Create a Trusted Launch VM with az vm create --security-type TrustedLaunch --enable-secure-boot true --enable-vtpm true; updating Secure Boot or vTPM on an existing VM triggers a reboot.
Trusted Launch doesn't increase VM pricing; Managed Image and Linux VM hibernation aren't supported, and Gen1 VMs can be upgraded to Gen2 Trusted Launch.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Virtual machines > (VM) > Settings > Configuration > Security type (Secure Boot, vTPM, Integrity monitoring)

lab.title: Deploy a Trusted Launch VM with integrity monitoring
steps: In Cloud Shell run: az group create -n rg-tl-lab -l eastus

Run: az vm create -g rg-tl-lab -n vmTL1 --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_D2s_v5 --security-type TrustedLaunch --enable-secure-boot true --enable-vtpm true --enable-integrity-monitoring --generate-ssh-keys
In the portal open vmTL1 > Configuration and review the Security type section.
Open Extensions + applications and confirm the Guest Attestation extension is installed.
In Defender for Cloud, check the VM's recommendations for Secure Boot, vTPM and guest attestation.
lab.verify: The VM Overview shows security type Trusted launch with integrity monitoring Enabled, and the Guest Attestation extension is provisioned successfully.

objectives.summary: Azure Machine Configuration (formerly guest configuration) audits and optionally enforces settings inside Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers, delivered through Azure Policy. Azure VMs need the Machine Configuration extension and a system-assigned managed identity, which the 'Deploy prerequisites to enable Guest Configuration policies on virtual machines' initiative deploys at scale. Arc servers already include the agent. Assignment types control whether settings are only audited, applied once and monitored, or automatically corrected.

keyFacts.fact: Azure VMs need the machine configuration extension and a system-assigned managed identity; Arc-enabled servers don't need the extension because it's included in the Connected Machine agent.

Assign the initiative 'Deploy prerequisites to enable Guest Configuration policies on virtual machines' to a management group, subscription or resource group to deploy the extension and identity at scale.

Assignment types: Audit (report only), ApplyAndMonitor (apply once, then report drift without correcting), ApplyAndAutoCorrect (apply and correct drift at the next evaluation). The property is case sensitive.
Configurations that change machines use the DeployIfNotExists effect; selecting Create a remediation task during assignment applies the configuration to existing noncompliant machines.
The machine configuration agent can't exceed 5% CPU, for both built-in and custom definitions, and the same limit applies to the service in the Arc Connected Machine agent.
Machine Configuration supports up to 50 guest assignments per machine, and per-setting results appear on the Guest assignments page.
Defender for Servers Plan 2 uses the Machine Configuration extension to assess OS configuration against Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark compute baselines.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Policy > Definitions (Category: Guest Configuration) > Assign; Azure portal > Policy > Guest assignments

lab.title: Deploy Machine Configuration prerequisites and assign a baseline audit
steps: In the Azure portal go to Policy > Definitions and search for the initiative 'Deploy prerequisites to enable Guest Configuration policies on virtual machines'.
Assign it to a test resource group, select Create a remediation task on the Remediation tab, and create the assignment.
Search for a built-in Guest Configuration audit definition, for example one auditing Windows machines against the Azure compute security baseline, and assign it to the same resource group.
Wait for evaluation, then open Policy > Guest assignments.
Select the VM's guest assignment and review the per-setting compliance results.
